title: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Offshore | MPI, US Gulf
description: On-site magnetic particle inspection for Gulf of Mexico platforms and yards: jacket welds, crane pedestals and lifting gear to AWS D1.1. Request an MT quote.
h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Offshore Platforms and Yards in the United States
html:
Magnetic particle inspection (MPI) is the fastest way to find surface cracks in the ferromagnetic steel that makes up most offshore structure: weld toes on jacket and deck framing, crane pedestals and booms, padeyes and lifting gear, and welded attachments on risers and vessels. Atlantis mobilizes technicians for offshore and Gulf Coast yard work in the United States; request an MT inspection quote with your weld maps or lifting-equipment list and we will scope it.

Where MT fits on offshore steel

Offshore assets are built from carbon and low-alloy steel, and that is exactly what MT examines well. The method magnetizes the part, applies fine iron particles, and shows cracks as particle lines because the leaking field gathers them. It finds surface-breaking and shallow subsurface cracks in welds, forgings and castings, including cracks too tight for the eye. It does not find internal flaws or measure wall loss, so a thickness question belongs to ultrasonic testing for offshore, and nonmagnetic alloys such as stainless tubing and aluminum helideck plate belong to liquid penetrant testing for offshore.

Regulations and codes behind offshore MT scopes

In the Gulf of Mexico Outer Continental Shelf, the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement regulates operations under 30 CFR Part 250, and each operator keeps a safety and environmental management system that ties inspection to structures and equipment. Structural integrity programs commonly follow API RP 2A and the related API structural integrity management guidance. Fabricated steel is examined to AWS D1.1, and topsides piping and vessels follow ASME B31.3 and ASME Section VIII. Cranes are governed by API Spec 2C and inspected under API RP 2D, and lifting appliances follow the ASME B30 series. The MT method itself is set out in ASME Section V Article 7, and ASTM E709 is the common practice standard.

Acceptance criteria come from the structural code or the operator's specification. Our technician reports indications; the operator's inspector decides whether a crack is acceptable or must be repaired.

Critical offshore MT targets

  • Weld toes on jacket nodes and deck framing at joints that see fatigue loading from waves and equipment. Where tubular joints are accessible above water, MT of the toe is a standard check.
  • Crane pedestals, booms and slewing structure: welds on the pedestal and boom are fatigue-prone and are called out in API RP 2D inspection programs, along with hooks and boom foot pins.
  • Padeyes, lifting lugs and spreader bars used for equipment lifts and platform installation, covered in more detail on the lifting equipment inspection page.
  • Riser clamps, supports and welded attachments on carbon steel pipe and vessels, where a crack in an attachment weld can lead to leakage.
  • Steel helideck framing and stair towers at their welded connections.
  • Structural repairs and new fabrication at Gulf Coast yards, covered by magnetic particle weld inspection.

How MT is adapted to offshore conditions

Offshore is a harsh environment for a method that depends on fine powder and clean surfaces. Wind blows dry particles away, so dry powder is used in sheltered corners or with windshields, and wet suspension is favored in the open. Salt spray and rain wash the surface and wet the particles, so white contrast paint is applied before the black particles are sprayed, and the surface is dried between steps. Daylight offshore is often too bright for fluorescent examination, so fluorescent work is done in a shaded area or at night with a black light and a tent; visible particles on a contrast background are the practical field choice.

Surface preparation is the first job. Marine growth, rust scale, paint and grease come off the weld and a band of base metal beside it, to the cleanliness the procedure specifies. Corroded or pitted surfaces trap particles and create false indications, so the technician distinguishes particle buildup at a pit from a linear crack indication and re-examines doubtful areas after light dressing. Electromagnetic yokes are the usual offshore tool because they are portable, need no cables to the structure and avoid the arcing that prods can cause around hydrocarbon systems; the procedure sets the lifting force the yoke must demonstrate, and the technician checks it before use.

Technique details: field direction and coverage

A crack is found only if the magnetic field crosses it, so each weld is examined twice with the yoke placed across the weld in two directions roughly at right angles. Tubular welds and weld toes with changing curvature need more yoke positions to maintain overlap, and the coverage is documented. The technician confirms the field strength with a gauge, applies particles while the field is on, and observes during and just after application. For wet fluorescent work, the black light intensity at the surface and the ambient white light level are measured and recorded, because they decide whether a faint indication would be seen.

Checks on the technique run through the shift. The wet particle concentration is verified with a settling test when the bath is mixed, the yoke is proven against a standard weight at the start of the day, and a reference indicator, such as a shim or ring standard, is used to show that the field and particles are working on the actual surface. If the temperature of a deck in the sun climbs past the range the procedure allows, the work stops and resumes in the shade or after the steel cools, because hot steel dries the suspension and weakens the indications.

Fatigue, hydrogen and installation damage to look for

Cracks on offshore steel come from a few recognizable sources. Fatigue cracks start at weld toes and sharp transitions under repeated wave and equipment loading, and they grow from the surface inward, which is exactly what MT is good at finding early. Hydrogen-assisted cracking appears in thick, high-strength or poorly preheated welds, sometimes hours or days after welding, so structural specifications often call for a delay before final examination. Installation and handling damage, such as gouges, arc strikes and cracked lifting lugs after a heavy lift, shows up at the first inspection after the event.

The report ties each finding to its likely cause where the pattern is clear, a toe crack along the weld edge, a transverse crack across the weld face, or a line at a fusion boundary, so the operator's engineer can judge whether it is a one-off fabrication defect or a sign of service loading. We state what we saw and where, and the engineer draws the conclusion about mechanism and remaining service.

Inspecting lifting gear before and after campaigns

Platform cranes and portable lifting gear work hard, and operators inspect them on a schedule driven by the manufacturer, the operator's program and API RP 2D. MT is part of that scope for critical components: the hook and its shank, boom foot pins and brackets, pad eyes, shackle bows where the specification allows, and the welds on the boom and pedestal. We examine to the component list the operator gives us, mark each item with its identification, and photograph indications. Items that must remain in service are tagged by the operator, and the decision to retire or repair stays with the operator's competent person.

After the examination, indications that are not relevant, such as a particle line at a sharp but sound geometric corner, are noted and explained rather than silently dropped, so a reviewer can follow how each mark on the weld was classified. Parts that were magnetized heavily are demagnetized when later welding or instrument fitting could be affected.

What to send for an offshore MT quote

  • Platform location or yard address and whether work is offshore or onshore
  • Weld maps, structural drawings or the lifting equipment list with ratings
  • Material and thickness, the code and the acceptance criteria
  • Coating status and who removes it, and access method such as scaffolding or a work basket
  • The operator's transport, safety training and permit requirements
  • Site contact and any security or badging requirements

Offshore planning: transport, safety and weather

The operator decides how people reach a platform, how many may be on board and what safety training they need. That can include offshore survival or helicopter underwater egress training, depending on the operator and the transport. We raise the question at the quote stage and arrange the requirements with the operator; we do not assume any certification. Technicians travel to your site, onshore or offshore, for the agreed scope, and weather often delays helicopter and boat schedules, so allow float days in an offshore campaign. At onshore yards, heat, humidity and rain affect particle application and light levels, and the work is staged under shelter where possible.

Where we work in the US for offshore

  • Houston: operator engineering offices and the largest pool of Gulf fabrication shops and lifting-equipment suppliers.
  • New Orleans: Louisiana's shelf operations and the supply bases that move crews and materials offshore.
  • Mobile: Alabama shipyards and offshore fabrication, with heavy structural and marine welding.
  • Lake Charles: heavy fabrication and repair near the Calcasieu Ship Channel.
  • Corpus Christi: Texas coast yards and ports serving Gulf and offshore wind-related steel.
  • Pascagoula: Mississippi's shipbuilding and marine fabrication base on the Gulf Coast.

Training your own MT technicians

Operators and fabricators building in-house MT teams can use MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training, with practice on the magnetic particle simulator, and the oil and gas NDT training page for the wider route. The employer certifies its technicians under its own written practice. National background: magnetic particle testing services and the MT complete guide.

What we do not do

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, does not run in-line inspection tools and does not offer underwater inspection or specialist techniques outside MT, PT and UT. We do not set inspection intervals or decide whether a crack is acceptable for continued service; the operator's engineer does that from our report.

faq.q: Which offshore components are best inspected by magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: Carbon steel weld toes on jacket and deck framing, crane pedestals and booms, padeyes and lifting lugs, riser clamps and welded attachments. MT finds surface cracks quickly on these ferromagnetic parts.
Not by us. Atlantis examines above-water structure and onshore equipment on platforms and in yards, while underwater magnetic particle inspection is a diver specialty that we do not offer.

faq.q: How do you handle wind and salt spray when using MT offshore?
faq.a: We use wet particle suspension in the open, shelter the area with windshields or tents, apply white contrast paint over the cleaned weld, and dry the surface between steps. Dry powder is used only in sheltered locations.

faq.q: Which codes govern offshore MT work?
faq.a: BSEE 30 CFR Part 250 regulates Gulf operations, API RP 2A and API Spec 2C and RP 2D guide platform and crane inspection, AWS D1.1 covers structural welds and ASME Section V Article 7 sets the method.

faq.q: Do you inspect cranes and lifting gear?
faq.a: Yes, the critical welds, hooks, pins and lugs identified in the crane manufacturer's manual and the operator's API RP 2D program. We report indications; the crane's competent person or operator decides on service.

faq.q: Who decides whether a crack is rejectable?
faq.a: Our Level II technician reports and evaluates indications against the named criteria. The operator's inspector or engineer makes the rejection and repair decision, and an ASNT Level III approves our procedure.

faq.q: What offshore safety training is required of your technicians?
faq.a: It depends on the operator and the transport, and may include offshore survival or helicopter egress training. We confirm the requirement at the quote stage and arrange it with the operator rather than claiming it in advance.

faq.q: What do you need for an offshore MT quote?
faq.a: The platform or yard location, weld maps or lifting-equipment list, material, code and acceptance criteria, coating and access details, and the operator's transport, permit and safety requirements.

faq.q: Is MT or PT better for offshore welds?
faq.a: MT is faster and more sensitive on carbon steel, so it is the first choice for structure and lifting gear. PT is used on stainless, duplex and aluminum, which are not magnetic.
